content: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has classified anthrax as a Category A biological warfare agent, indicating its substantial potential to negatively impact public health. 3. The lethality of aerosolized Bacillus anthracis spores was demonstrated in 1979 when an accidental release from a military microbiology facility in the former Soviet Union resulted in 64 deaths. 4. The anthrax cases that occurred in 2001, following the distribution of Bacillus anthracis spores through the U.S. mail, highlighted the organism's potential as a bioterrorism threat. 5. Vaccines against anthrax were first developed in the 1880s and were initially used in livestock. 6. Anthrax is a zoonotic disease caused by the spore-forming bacterium Bacillus anthracis. It primarily affects wild and domestic mammals, such as cattle, sheep, goats, camels, antelope, and other herbivores. 7. 8. cutaneous, gastrointestinal, or inhalation. 9. Bacillus anthracis is a facultatively anaerobic, gram-positive, encapsulated, spore-forming, nonmotile rod. Its infectious form in the environment is the spore, which is highly resistant to heat, cold, drought, UV light, and gamma radiation. 10. Bacillus anthracis has three major virulence factors: an antiphagocytic capsule and two exotoxins, lethal toxin and edema toxin, which are responsible for clinical manifestations such as hemorrhage, edema, necrosis, and death. 11. cutaneous, gastrointestinal, or inhalation. 12. 13. Based on nonhuman primate studies, the lethal dose of Bacillus anthracis spores is estimated to range from 2,500 to 760,000 spores. 14. Most human anthrax cases worldwide occur naturally and are not the result of bioterrorism. 15. The case-fatality rate for anthrax varies widely, from less than 1% for treated cutaneous anthrax to 86%-89% for inhalation anthrax during outbreaks in the Soviet Union and the United States. 16. 17. Bacillus anthracis spores can remain viable and infectious in soil for decades, posing a risk to grazing livestock that ingest or inhale the spores. 18. Agricultural anthrax cases occur among individuals who have direct contact with infected animals or their carcasses, such as ranchers, veterinarians, slaughterhouse workers, and butchers. 19. Industrial anthrax cases result from cutaneous inoculation or inhalation of Bacillus anthracis spores during the processing of contaminated animal hides, hair, or wool. 20. Workers in wool and mohair processing facilities were historically at risk for both inhalation and cutaneous anthrax, making the disease a significant health hazard in the wool industry during the 19th and early 20th centuries. 21. Naturally occurring anthrax cases have also been linked to contact with products from infected animals, such as contaminated shaving brushes, animal skins, hair, yarn, and bone meal. 22. Estimating the global incidence of naturally occurring human anthrax is challenging due to unreliable reporting in many regions. 23. Anthrax is most commonly observed in agricultural regions with inadequate control programs for livestock anthrax, leading to human infections. 24. Enzootic and endemic regions for anthrax include South America, Central America, southern and eastern Europe, Asia, Africa, the Caribbean, and the Middle East. 25. The largest recent human anthrax epidemic occurred in Zimbabwe between 1978 and 1980, involving 9,445 cases and 141 deaths. 26. In the United States, the incidence of anthrax in animals has decreased significantly since the mid-20th century, with outbreaks now primarily reported in the Great Plains and western states. 27. Sporadic cases of anthrax in domestic livestock and wildlife may go unrecognized. 28. Anthrax is a nationally notifiable disease in the United States, with naturally occurring human cases reported sporadically, typically two or fewer per year. 29. Of the 242 naturally occurring human anthrax cases reported to the CDC between 1955 and 2007, 96% were cutaneous, 4% were inhalation, and none were gastrointestinal. 30. 31. In 2001, 22 confirmed or suspected human anthrax cases occurred in the eastern United States due to Bacillus anthracis spores sent through the mail. Eleven cases were inhalation anthrax, and five individuals with inhalation anthrax died. 32. Bacillus anthracis has been a focus of offensive and defensive biological warfare research programs worldwide, with documented use as a bioweapon during World War I and World War II. 33. In 1979, an anthrax outbreak in Sverdlovsk, Soviet Union, resulted in at least 96 infections and 64 deaths following the unintentional release of Bacillus anthracis spores from a military microbiology facility. 34. In 1993, the Aum Shinrikyo cult unsuccessfully attempted to use Bacillus anthracis as a weapon near Tokyo, Japan. 35. The Department of Homeland Security has identified anthrax as a significant threat to U.S. national security. 36. WHO experts estimate that the release of 50 kg of Bacillus anthracis spores upwind of a population center of 500,000 people could result in 95,000 deaths and 125,000 hospitalizations. 37. Intentionally dispersed strains of Bacillus anthracis may exhibit antimicrobial resistance or enhanced dispersion capabilities, posing additional challenges in bioterrorism scenarios. 38. 39. 40. The pathogenicity of Bacillus anthracis is primarily due to the combined actions of its antiphagocytic capsule and two protein exotoxins, edema toxin and lethal toxin, which disrupt immune responses and cause tissue damage. 41. Cutaneous anthrax, the most common form of the disease, is associated with handling infected animals or contaminated products. It typically presents as a painless necrotic ulcer with a characteristic black eschar. 42. Gastrointestinal anthrax occurs after consuming contaminated meat and can manifest as intestinal or oropharyngeal forms, with symptoms ranging from mild gastrointestinal disturbances to severe systemic illness. 43. Inhalation anthrax, a systemic infection caused by inhaling Bacillus anthracis spores, is characterized by nonspecific early symptoms followed by severe respiratory distress, shock, and high mortality rates if untreated.
